title: Zeta potential of magnetic-field-controlled silver nanoparticles
abstract: Magnetic-field-dependent nanoparticle size does not by itself determine zeta potential, which also depends on interfacial charge, electrolyte screening, and the location of the slipping plane. We extend the sphere-packing description of silver nanoparticles by distinguishing the structural surface, the effective charge plane, and the hydrodynamic slipping plane. The model uses structural radii of \SI{20}{nm} and \SI{5}{nm} at zero field and \SI{250}{mT}, with reported zeta potentials of \SI{-13.2}{mV} and \SI{-10.0}{mV}. Effective charge is related to the defective-shell atom count. For field-independent interfacial parameters, the linear response without additional charge weighting decreases with decreasing radius. Its normalized form depends on three electrokinetic lengths through only two sums, preventing their independent determination from a field-dependent zeta curve. At \((κ^{-1},t_{\mathrm{lig}},δ_{\mathrm{slip}})=(3,0,1)\,\mathrm{nm}\), nonlinear Poisson--Boltzmann electrostatics changes the fitted shell coefficient from 0.316 to 0.299. Constant total charge still predicts an increase in zeta magnitude, opposite to the observed trend in the evaluated scenarios. Independently calibrated shell and area charge laws differ by less than \SI{0.05}{mV}, so the endpoint agreement does not distinguish these mechanisms. Propagating the initial size frequencies gives a narrower endpoint size distribution than measured. With charge parameters determined from the measured size populations, its predicted mean zeta potential is \SI{-9.131}{mV}, with standard deviation \SI{0.994}{mV}. Imposing the measured mean by charge recalibration does not remove the discrepancy in size width. The combined structural and electrokinetic model thus identifies both the size-dependent contribution to zeta potential and the interfacial information needed to interpret it.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theoretical model to calculate the zeta potential of silver nanoparticles whose size is controlled by an applied magnetic field. It overcomes the limitation that size alone is insufficient by integrating structural size evolution with detailed electrokinetic theory. The resulting model provides a robust framework for interpreting the relationship between nanoparticle structure and colloidal stability.
main_problem: The study aims to accurately determine the zeta potential of silver nanoparticles whose size is controlled by an external magnetic field, recognizing that size alone is insufficient for this prediction.
main_result: The combined structural and electrokinetic model successfully identifies both the size-dependent contribution to the zeta potential and the necessary interfacial information required for its correct interpretation.
method: The authors extend the sphere-packing description by distinguishing three radii (structural, effective charge, and hydrodynamic slipping plane) and applying the Poisson-Boltzmann electrostatics.
model_or_system: The system involves silver nanoparticles whose size distribution is governed by magnetic-field-controlled nucleation theory. The model couples this structural input to an electrokinetic calculation that determines the potential at the hydrodynamic slipping plane.
key_observables: Zeta potential ($\zeta$), structural radius, effective charge, and the location of the slipping plane.
important_parameters: Magnetic field strength ($B$), Debye screening length ($\kappa^{-1}$), and the various geometric offsets ($\delta_{slip}$, $t_{lig}$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes spherical symmetry, a symmetric monovalent electrolyte, and that the structural size distribution dictates the input for the electrokinetic calculation.
figures_summary: Figures compare cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of particle sizes and potentials across varying magnetic fields, illustrating the structural propagation method and potential magnitude calculations.
paper_structure:
The paper progresses by first establishing the physical limitations (size $
eq$ zeta potential), then developing a comprehensive model that integrates structural size selection with electrokinetic theory, and finally validating the model using numerical checks and comparisons against measured data.
why_interesting: While focused on colloid science, the rigorous coupling of structural evolution (nucleation) with an electrostatic potential calculation demonstrates a complex, multi-scale physical modeling approach applicable to systems where geometry dictates emergent properties.
